extracted.intended_audience: EPA stakeholders, technical commenters, risk assessors, and regulated entities concerned with the 2024 CCR Risk Assessment and groundwater modeling
extracted.subtask_short: EPA CCR groundwater risk assessment modeling
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for building, documenting, and defending groundwater fate-and-transport and leaching modeling used in EPA's 2024 CCR (coal combustion residuals) Risk Assessment; includes conceptual-model choices, data sources, modeling tools, and uncertainty characterization. Intended to guide reviewers and commenters on whether modeling choices are appropriate for national regulatory decisionmaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disposal below the water table
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual models for landfills and surface impoundments did not evaluate contact with groundwater because the scenario could not be incorporated into groundwater fate and transport modeling as a result of data and model constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inability to model a practice exists, explicitly acknowledge that risk estimates may underestimate risks nationally. When possible, clarify the scope (i.e., the scenario was acknowledged but not modeled) and discuss the implications for underestimation of risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ponded water vs porewater and residual water impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceptual model should clarify the distinction between water ponded above the ash and porewater within an impoundment, and recognize that any free liquids that remain within the unit can still result in higher leakage than if the unit were fully dewatered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model hydraulic head and leakage potential for residual water; note that drained units may remain substantially saturated (examples cited: closed impoundments remain saturated by 20–54 feet). Use lifecycle stage considerations to focus on the period contributing most to long-term risk (e.g., operation when wastewater is ponded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus conceptual models on the lifecycle stage contributing most to long-term risk
rubrics_metrics.description: For surface impoundments, the most relevant stage for long-term risk is when the units are in operation due to wastewater ponded above ash; subsequent draining does not remediate adverse impacts that occurred during operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize modeling scenarios and assumptions for the life-stage that drives long-term releases and exposures rather than later states that do not remove prior impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include relevant CCRMU fill configurations where data permit
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptual model for CCRMU fills should address concentrated footprints (e.g., placement beneath parking lots) and the types of placements that are within regulatory scope; diffuse or infrequent placements should be identified but may not be modeled if no data exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When data on manner or frequency of placements are lacking, document the resulting uncertainty but still identify where such placements have occurred because even small placements can contribute to leakage and influence nearby groundwater monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of representative, recent environmental data (HELP/weather)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2024 Risk Assessment incorporated more recent weather data available from the most recent version of the Hydrologic Evaluation of Landfill Performance (HELP) model (updated 2020) while relying on other data sources previously found to be representative nationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify data currency and representativeness for national-scale modeling; explain why older data remain appropriate or incorporate new data where it meaningfully changes results and is supported by further modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use laboratory LEAF leaching tests to estimate long-term leaching potential
rubrics_metrics.description: LEAF laboratory leaching tests (e.g., Method 1313) are effective for estimating field leaching behavior for a wide range of materials under disposal and use conditions and provide data on individual CCR leaching across environmental conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LEAF for long-term leaching potential of individual CCRs, but apply recommended adjustments (e.g., liquid-to-solid ratio corrections and geochemical speciation for redox-sensitive contaminants). Where LEAF data are lacking for specific constituents, consider supplemental data but document limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer LEAF leachate over pooled field leachate for fills when representative field data are scarce
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little field leachate data for dry-managed CCR; LEAF provides leaching behavior of individual CCR under a range of conditions and so is the most realistic estimate of long-term leaching for CCR placed in fills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limitations of field datasets (mixtures of wastes, unknown sampling history) and prefer standardized laboratory methods for national probabilistic modeling; supplement with field data only when adequately representative and well documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust LEAF-based inputs for highly soluble and redox-sensitive constituents
rubrics_metrics.description: LEAF Method 1313 can (1) underestimate leakage of highly soluble constituents if not adjusted for liquid-to-solid ratio and (2) over- or underestimate redox-sensitive contaminants (e.g., arsenic) if not coupled with geochemical speciation modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Agency general recommendations for addressing these issues in constructing model inputs and document adjustments applied in risk runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret probabilistic percentiles correctly (inputs vs modeled risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 90th percentile of all model inputs for leachate concentration is not the same as the 90th percentile of modeled risks; other parameters (release, transport) influence downgradient concentrations such that the runs with highest inputs are not always highest risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid equating high percentile input parameter values with high-end risk outcomes; analyze full model outputs and review representative model runs around the percentile-of-interest (e.g., 90th percentile risk results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive modeled leachate pH from ash 'own pH' when fills are single-source
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeled leachate pH is based on the natural pH ('own pH') of the ash sample measured with LEAF; for smaller CCRMU fills likely constructed with a single ash type, it is most appropriate to consider individual ash pH rather than average landfill pH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sample-specific pH for single-source fills and discuss uncertainties in pH modeling (see Risk Assessment Section 6). Recognize that landfill averages may mask acidic regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and set sampling radii for environmental and population data
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA reviewed and updated the sampling radius for environmental data to two kilometers (1.2 miles), consistent with methodology applied in the 2014 Risk Assessment; sampling radii for population data were established consistent with the rationale in the 2024 Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document rationale for chosen sampling radii, maintain consistency with prior methods when appropriate, and update when new review supports a change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model sorption using sorption isotherms/distributions rather than single Kd values
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA developed sorption isotherms for each modeled constituent that represent distributions of individual Kd values reflecting anticipated subsurface conditions and specific CCR waste characteristics; EPACMTP samples from that distribution per model run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture variability by sampling from full distributions in probabilistic runs; do not rely solely on single representative Kd values for national-scale probabilistic modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MODFLOW Kd values to represent targeted high-end scenarios when performing limited MODFLOW runs
rubrics_metrics.description: The limited number of MODFLOW runs are intended to further characterize the subset of high-end scenarios modeled in EPACMTP, so it is reasonable these MODFLOW runs may reflect scenarios where pentavalent arsenic is more mobile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using a reduced set of runs in computationally intensive models, select runs that characterize the high-end or scenario-of-interest and document how those runs map to the broader probabilistic distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model hydraulic conductivity based on dominant soil megatexture and account for disturbance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because compaction and future disturbances can change permeability, EPA modeled conductivity based on the dominant soil megatexture and assumed ash had been subjected to a similar degree of compaction as surrounding soil, rather than defining a fixed probabilistic distribution of conductivities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative soil megatexture inputs, justify compaction assumptions, and explicitly discuss uncertainty from potential disturbances (human, animals, weather, freeze-thaw, flooding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume widespread pozzolanic reduction of conductivity without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Although some fly ash is pozzolanic, commenters provided no information about how common that ash is in CCRMU fills or about long-term conductivity when left exposed; therefore EPA did not assume reduced hydraulic conductivity based on pozzolanic behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require data documenting prevalence and long-term field behavior before assuming reduced conductivity from pozzolanic reactions in probabilistic modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporate newer infiltration/weather analyses only with supporting modeling refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2023 Draft Risk Assessment indicated potential higher infiltration for certain soil types using new HELP data, but EPA did not conduct additional modeling because prior 2014 results were sufficient for the rulemaking; thus the particular analysis was not included in the 2024 Risk Assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If new data suggest materially different results (e.g., higher infiltration), perform the needed additional modeling to refine the analysis before relying on it for regulatory decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select constituents for groundwater modeling based on prior identified risk drivers and data availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Constituents selected were those found to be risk drivers for unlined surface impoundments in the 2014 Risk Assessment; some additional constituents lacked health benchmarks and so could not be quantitatively evaluated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose constituents using prior risk-driver evidence and availability of health benchmarks; document why other constituents were excluded and discuss uncertainties in selection (see Risk Assessment Section 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify modeling horizon and stopping rules (e.g., up to 10,000 years)
rubrics_metrics.description: Groundwater models were run until observed concentration reached a peak and fell below a minimum concentration (1 × 10^-16 mg/L), or the model ran for 10,000 years — the same maximum horizon used in 2014 — and longer horizons are informative because inorganic contaminants persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the stopping criteria, explain that reaching the maximum horizon does not imply all runs take that long, and discuss implications for time-to-first-exceedance and duration of contamination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider interception by surface water where representative data exist; document rationale when omitted
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA did not explicitly evaluate interception by surface water because facilities generally have not maintained reliable records of fill locations and thus representative probabilistic distributions of distances to downgradient water bodies could not be developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interceptive processes are omitted due to lack of data, explain why and assess whether omission materially affects high-end risk conclusions; document that interception typically reduces median risks but may not affect high-end modeled risks driving regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model both lined and unlined units and consider national prevalence and liner performance issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk assessments modeled both lined and unlined units; national criteria must evaluate the full range of conditions and final requirements are driven by higher-end risks associated with unlined units, particularly given evidence some engineered liners have already entered corrective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include prevalence estimates of liner status in national modeling, account for liner performance failures, and justify regulatory choices based on the range of modeled conditions and statutory standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model exposures at appropriate receptor distances (waste boundary vs offsite mile)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2024 Risk Assessment modeled contamination extent to the waste boundary for smaller CCRMU fills; concentrations and risks nearer the waste boundary can reasonably be higher than offsite values modeled up to a mile in prior assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select receptor distances consistent with the exposure scenario of interest (e.g., onsite/waste-boundary receptors for fills) and explain why comparisons to prior offsite-focused results may not be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when comparing modeled concentrations to field monitoring data
rubrics_metrics.description: Field monitoring data vary by age, operational status and well placement; improperly installed or spaced wells and averaging across a landfill footprint can mask localized high concentrations, so direct comparisons to model runs may be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representativeness of monitoring datasets (sampling locations relative to waste boundary, sample timing and frequency, site heterogeneity) before using monitoring to validate or invalidate modeled results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose sampling depth and along-plume location consistent with modeling goals
rubrics_metrics.description: EPACMTP sampled along the centerline of the plume and to a depth of five feet in order to identify potential magnitude of Groundwater Protection Standard (GWPS) exceedances at the waste boundary and support further MODFLOW modeling; this differs from 2014 which sampled the top 30 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and justify the sampling depth and lateral location choices in the context of the receptor and modeling objectives; explain why different depth choices may be more or less relevant for comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select groundwater model type and mode consistent with process goals (MODFLOW-USG rationale)
rubrics_metrics.description: MODFLOW-USG was selected for its ability to simulate flow and transport in both unsaturated and saturated zones without additional packages and to simulate flow and transport sequentially; steady-state simulations were not used because they do not provide time series plume evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose modeling platforms that can represent needed physical processes (e.g., unsaturated zone, transient behavior), justify the choice versus alternatives (e.g., MODFLOW6), and avoid steady-state approaches where time evolution is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate model documentation while accounting for practical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA reviewed model documentation to ensure relevant information raised by commenters was clear; full output files for all MODFLOW runs were not incorporated due to prohibitive file size, but documentation level was consistent with EPACMTP and typos corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient documentation of inputs, methods, and representative outputs to allow evaluation; if full outputs are infeasible to publish, explain why and provide alternative accessible summaries and ensure consistency and error-correction (e.g., fix reported typos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and discuss uncertainties explicitly when data are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Where little data exist (e.g., diffuse placements, prevalence/magnitude of reducing conditions), the 2024 Risk Assessment did not model those scenarios and acknowledged this as a source of uncertainty discussed in Section 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When not modeling due to data gaps, explicitly state the uncertainty, describe potential directions of bias (under/overestimate), and indicate where additional data could change conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure statistical summaries and plotted model outputs are correct and robust before drawing conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: An EPA graph from the Draft Risk Assessment incorrectly summarized model results by combining age cohorts; upon review EPA found filtering to relevant subsets produced relatively few runs and thus the graph was not used as a line of evidence for the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify filtering, aggregation, and sample sizes supporting plotted summaries; avoid using summaries based on insufficient runs to draw national-scale conclusions or to define thresholds (e.g., a unit-size cutoff).
